items.title: Reverse Splitter Cycle Update 2: I have made an initial decision
items.text:
Reverse Splitter Cycle Update 2: I have made an initial decision
Applied: early to mid January

Acceptances: UCLA (30% tuition scholarship), Boston College (60% tuition scholarship), Boston University (60% tuition scholarship), George Mason (100% tuition scholarship), Emory (90% tuition scholarship)

Waitlists: Georgetown, Cornell, UPenn, Northwestern, UVA, GW

Rejections: Chicago, Michigan, Berkeley

Still waiting on: NYU

I visited Emory, liked what I saw, and decided to go with that. Still riding out every waitlist except for GW, but if there's no movement or even if I get in and it doesn't prove to be financially viable, I'll be happy with Emory.

What do you all think?
Law

I really don't think it's that much on the table. After crunching the numbers for the Classes of 2018, I found that UCLA and BU send about 44% and 46% of graduates to 100+ associate firms, which is indeed more than Emory does at about 34%, but I don't think that 10-12% increase justifies shelling out more cash for either of those schools, especially taking into account the costs of living at them. Big Law is still not a sure thing at either of those schools, and going to them ties my hands as far as what I can do after law school significantly more than Emory would because of the increased debt. Basically, if I do well at Emory, the world still opens up to me, but at the same time if I do a mediocre job there my life isn't ruined because the debt I incur will be manageable even on a salary of around $50k per year. I don't have that freedom at these other schools. 

I'm not eyeing federal clerkships much either but Emory happens to have the highest percentage of federal clerkships out of the three from 2018 as well, with 4.85% of its class doing those as opposed to 4.38% at UCLA and 2.65% at BU. 

I was being kind of a wise guy when I said my goal is "Law" but there's some truth to that in that I'm keeping my options open with a lean towards corporate.

I’m going to offer a different take to a lot of people on this sub and say “probably not.” For the reason that a lot of people analyze this from solely the perspective of  “higher LSAT = better chance,” which is obviously true, but maybe not the smartest way to look at things. 

In reality, I think it’s a lot of suffering to put yourself through even before test day and then it’s only worth it if everything *does* pan out on test day. If you have an off day, it’s weeks of prep all up in smoke. 

You have good offers from good schools. Sometimes, less phenomenal (but still decent) career outcomes with less debt (remember, it’s not the norm to get $$ off the waitlist) are more sensible than even getting into low T14 at sticker and then having to do Big Law for several years just to be at the point of financially breaking even. Spivey had an article about this, basically how a substantial scholarship at T30 can often be a more sensible choice than T14 at sticker. 

I’d say the bottom line here is, if you have nothing better to do for the time being, take that June exam. If you have anything else you think might be more productive, or even just want to enjoy an easier life before the Fall semester, don’t do it.

items.title: How every moment of a self-guided tour of a school that waitlisted you feels
items.text: How every moment of a self-guided tour of a school that waitlisted you feels
I did not but now I wonder why you asked

From what I've seen at the schools I have visited that waitlisted me the treatment is pretty standard, but I understand why they do that. You don't want people to think that increasingly large and frequent displays of enthusiasm are the way to get in because that probably leads to a very annoyed admissions committee.

Admitted students events are less awkward in that everyone's there for the same reason and people are actually looking to talk whereas on the self-guided tour you basically just look like a rando wanderer
Oh that makes sense. Lucky for me I was able to catch guided tours at the schools I was admitted to so it was a different experience, a lot more welcoming
The way I know that’s a real story is that it didn’t end with “And then he admitted me on the spot. And everyone in the room clapped.”

items.title: Final decision of the cycle: NYU WL
items.text:
Final decision of the cycle: NYU WL
Applied in the beginning of January. Saw this coming. Definitely going to wait it out.

There's no bad choice here, you're dealing with two widely respected schools which both have great placement in NYC. There's something to be said about the discomfort of adjusting to a new environment and the potential benefit of staying at your undergrad alma mater for law school to make for less of an adjustment period, especially considering how they admitted you to an interesting program to boot. At the end of the day though, you really just have to follow your gut.

Turning down any offer is hard, even an objectively bad one, in my experience. I had full tuition offers at lower Tier 1 schools that I turned down for slightly lower offers from objectively better schools, but I'm definitely conscious of the fact that 9 out of 10 people trying to enter this profession would do backflips to get the offers that I ended up turning down, and even more so with the offers that you're getting.

I have heard a bit about the T13 vs. T14 thing with GULC getting clowned on for having lower Big Law numbers than Vanderbilt, but at the same time I've heard a lot about how much GULC grads self select into fields like government and PI so maybe the numbers advantage really isn't all that vast at the end of the day.
